job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Erik Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at 8:30 at the Brenton Savings Bank, where I'm a trainee credit analyst on the small-business desk. I read loan applications, build cash-flow tables and write a one-page summary for my team lead, Ingrid. At lunch I walk to the canal with Tomas from the mortgage team. I finished my finance and economics degree top of the year in June, and I split a flat with my old uni friend Lasse. My dad drives a city bus and is a union rep, so work talk at our table is never boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, useful here and there but not a revolution. I use a chat assistant now and then to tidy a summary or explain an unfamiliar ratio, and I'd tell colleagues it's a decent intern. I'd also say we shouldn't let the hype set policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly I'd feel pretty safe. The bank still needs people who can read a baker's accounts and judge whether the baker is honest. A cash-flow table can be built by anyone, but deciding whether to lend to a nervous baker still takes a person who has met the baker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the credit training and finish the bank's internal exam by spring. I'd keep using the assistant for drafts, but I'd check every number myself. I'd also put about £200 a month into savings and my pension, which is something my dad nagged me about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, quite settled. It's a little boring, if I'm honest, but I like that. I'd get on with becoming good at the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or worry in your own life would stay exactly the same even if nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My student loan and my share of the rent, about £540. I also help my mum with her car insurance when she's short. Those would stay whatever AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your week is routine screen work that even a small change could touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fair bit, maybe a third of my day, is building the tables and writing first drafts. The assistant already speeds that up, so I'd expect Ingrid to want more applications per analyst. That's not scary, it just raises the targets.

say: I'd tell colleagues the chat assistant is a **decent intern**.
I'd say hype shouldn't drive **policy** or hiring.
I'd say the bank still needs people who **know** its customers.
think: I feel fairly **safe**, because lending needs judgement about real people.
About a third of my day is **drafting** that tools already speed up.
I expect **higher targets** per analyst rather than job cuts.
do: Finish the bank's internal credit **exam** by spring.
Check every **number** the assistant gives me myself.
Put **£200 a month** into savings and my pension.
feel: **Settled**, a little bored, and happy with that.
Quietly **confident** about the next couple of years.
S0.quote: A cash-flow table can be built by anyone, but deciding whether to lend to a nervous baker still takes a person who has met the baker.
fieldNote: Judges his work on the **people** side, not the table side.
Already uses AI **sometimes**, so his calm is informed.
His dad's **pension** nagging shows in his savings habit.

steps.text: Pass the bank's internal credit exam by spring
Use the chat assistant for first drafts and check every figure
Pay £200 a month into savings and my pension

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the bank should be open about it: what the software does, what stays with us, and what happens to hiring. Online I'd say regulators have to look at lending models before they're everywhere. I'd also tell my dad's union friends to start asking for a seat at the table now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my kind of job shrinks. My team lead Ingrid used to have four analysts, and next year the desk may need only two, plus software that writes the first draft of every loan file. I'm good, so I'd probably stay, but I'm among the newest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new underwriting software properly, because I'd rather be the person who understands how it decides. I'd ask to move onto the harder files, the ones with farms and small factories where numbers are messy. I'd also build up three months of savings instead of one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert more than scared. I feel a bit of a squeeze, like the ladder has fewer rungs. But I trust that I can adapt when I've seen it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Think of a task you did last week. Which part would software take over first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first-pass credit scoring. Right now I spend two days on a small-company file, and the software could produce the draft in minutes. My job would become checking its reasoning and talking to the customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your manager do differently about hiring people at your level?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd hire fewer graduates and promote the ones they have faster, which is good for me and bad for the next class. I'd also expect Ingrid to be asked to show savings in her budget, so one of us would not be replaced.

say: I'd say the bank should be **open** about what the software does.
I'd say regulators must examine **lending models** before they spread.
I'd tell my dad's union friends to ask for a **seat at the table**.
think: I think junior **analyst jobs** shrink, with fewer rungs on the ladder.
I'm good, so I'd probably **stay**, but I'm among the newest.
I'd rather understand how the software **decides** than be judged by it.
do: Ask for the harder **farm and factory** files where numbers are messy.
Raise my savings to **three months** of costs.
feel: **Alert** more than scared, like the ladder has fewer rungs.
Trust that I can **adapt** once things are proven.
S1.quote: My team lead Ingrid used to have four analysts, and next year the desk may need only two, plus software that writes the first draft of every loan file.
fieldNote: He plans to become the person who **understands** the tool.
Notes the **next class** will have it worse than him.
Union family background gives him a **collective** instinct.

steps.text: Learn the new underwriting software in detail
Ask Ingrid for the messier farm and small factory files
Build savings from one month to three months of costs
Write to my regional representative about lending-model rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for anyone to be ready, and that the government should have a plan by now. At work I'd keep it measured, but with my dad and his bus-union friends I'd say we need strong rules, quickly. I'd say that if firms save billions, some of it has to go to the people replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the junior part of banking disappears first. When the software can do the work of my whole desk, nobody will keep a 24-year-old around to learn on the side. I might be one of the people let go in a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop any non-essential spending and push savings from £200 to £400 a month. I'd try to move into a role that deals with clients face to face, like a branch business adviser, before the desk work goes. And I'd ask my parents whether I could move back in for a few months if I needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pressured. My stomach tightens when I picture telling Ingrid I know the task is going. It feels fast and out of my control, which I don't enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Say it's the day the announcement is made. What do you tell the people close to you that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad on the bus ride home that I think we're in for a rough few years. He'd say the union will fight, and mum would offer me my old room. I'd also tell Lasse we should think about whether to keep the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, what happens to the money you owe and the money you've saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan stays at the minimum payment and I keep cash. Savings go first to rent, then food. If I'm laid off, I'd rather have eight months of cash than a smaller loan.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** for anyone to be ready.
I'd tell my dad's union friends we need strong **rules** quickly.
I'd say firms that save billions must share some of it with **replaced** staff.
think: The junior part of banking likely **disappears first**, and I may be among those let go.
Nobody keeps a 24-year-old around to **learn** when software does the desk's work.
It feels fast and **out of my control**.
do: Raise savings from £200 to **£400 a month**.
Aim for a **face-to-face** client role, such as a branch adviser.
Ask my parents if I can **move back** for a few months if needed.
feel: **Pressured**, with a tight stomach about telling Ingrid.
**Frustrated** that the pace is out of my hands.
S2.quote: When the software can do the work of my whole desk, nobody will keep a 24-year-old around to learn on the side.
fieldNote: Moves from **trust** in adapting to a defensive money plan.
His family is a real **safety net**, which keeps him anxious rather than alarmed.

steps.text: Raise savings from £200 to £400 a month
Stop takeaways and the gym to cut spending hard
Apply for a branch adviser role that meets customers in person
Ask my parents to keep my old room ready

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is real time and it should be used to write the rules and build retraining. At work I'd ask what the bank's plan is for people like me. I'd tell friends that it's a good moment to learn the new tools before they're compulsory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel I have a chance. By 2031 I'd be 27 and have five years of credit experience, and that might be enough to move into something people-facing like advising or compliance. I'd still be nervous, but less than in the 2028 case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my banking exams and then start a part-time master's in risk. I'd use AI more every month so it's second nature, and I'd move to a bigger city bank if there's a role that trains people. I'd keep saving £300 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Careful and a little excited. I like having something to prepare for. I just have to avoid putting it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes about your plan with 5 years instead of 2?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I can still change the plan, so I'd rather spend the time learning than just saving. Two years only lets me panic and hold cash. Five lets me move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you do you think sees this coming, and who doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad sees it, and a few of the older analysts do. The graduates are split: half think it's hype, half are quietly doing online data courses. Ingrid is somewhere in between.

I'd ask the bank what its **plan** is for people like me.
I'd tell friends to learn the new tools **before** they're compulsory.
think: By 2031 I'd have five years of **experience** to move into advising or compliance.
I'd be nervous, but **less** than with two years.
I like having something to **prepare** for, if I don't put it off.
do: Finish the banking exams, then a part-time **risk** master's.
Use AI **more every month** so it feels natural.
feel: Glad there is **time**, wary of delay.
S3.quote: With five years I can still change the plan, so I'd rather spend the time learning than just saving.
fieldNote: Time converts **fear** into study plans for him, rather than into cash hoarding.
Knows his own risk is **delay**, and says so unprompted.
Splits peers into **hype** believers and quiet trainers.

steps.text: Start a part-time master's in risk management after the exams
Use the AI assistant on one work task every week
Apply to compliance or advising teams at a bigger bank

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get it right if people start now: retraining funds, new rules and a fair share of the gains. I'd tell friends that it's not a reason to switch off. I'd also say we shouldn't leave it to the banks to decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel fairly okay. By 2036 I'd be 32 with a decade in finance, and I'd have shifted into a job that needs judgement and trust. I'd worry more about the graduates who come after me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work up through credit to a relationship role, keep studying part-time, and join the union branch for bank staff, which exists but is quiet. I'd also learn to code a bit, like simple scripts for data. And I'd put money into an index fund each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic, with some guilt. I'd rather be 32 with a plan than 24 with a panic, but I worry about the graduate who starts after me. It's a fair deal for me and not for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, what would you start now that you wouldn't with 2 years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the part-time qualification now, not in five years. I'd also learn the basics of how the models are built, because understanding how the tool thinks keeps me useful. With two years I couldn't do any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At 32, what do you hope your working life looks like, and what could stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to lead a small team of analysts and a few apprentices who learn the trade properly. What could stop me is if the bank is merged and automated into one big model, and nobody is hired to learn at all.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to get it right if we **start now**.
I'd say gains from AI should be **shared** fairly.
I'd say the banks shouldn't be left to decide **alone**.
think: By 2036 I'd be 32 and in work needing **trust**.
I worry more about graduates who **follow** me.
Understanding how the tools think keeps me **useful**.
do: Join the quiet **union branch** for bank staff.
Start the part-time **qualification** now, not later.
Learn to **code** simple scripts and invest monthly in an index fund.
feel: **Optimistic**, with some guilt about those who come after.
S4.quote: I'd rather be 32 with a plan than 24 with a panic, but I worry about the graduate who starts after me.
fieldNote: A decade gives him **agency**, and his steady style suits it.
His concern turns to **fairness** for later graduates.
Wants **apprentices** to keep a path in.

steps.text: Start a part-time banking qualification this autumn
Learn simple scripts to handle credit data myself
Join the bank staff union branch and attend meetings
Put £100 a month into a low-cost index fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it's the only one where I run out of time. I'd want retraining funded by the firms that gain, a real say for staff in how banks use AI, and rules from the government before everything is already deployed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say I'm not afraid of the technology, I'm afraid of the speed. A good plan with a decade is a gift, but the same plan with two years is a crisis nobody is ready for. That's what I'd want leaders to understand.

headlineQuote: A good plan with a decade is a gift, but the same plan with two years is a crisis nobody is ready for.
portrait: Erik is a **22-year-old** trainee credit analyst at a regional bank, top of his finance class, sharing a flat with a friend.
He uses AI tools now and then and trusts new things once they're **proven**.
He is progressive and union-raised, so he wants **rules**, retraining and shared gains.
He stays calm in the mild case, becomes **anxious** at two years, and eases with five or ten.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because speed leaves no time to retrain or set rules.
whatWouldHelp: **Retraining** funded by firms that gain, staff say over bank AI use, and rules before launch.
